entries.title: fuzz the bounds-check elision with proofgen programs under ASan
entries.body:
CI's soundness step now compiles 600 fixed-seed programs from proofgen.js a second time with --no-elision, alongside the runnable cases and the fuzz corpus. Each program comes in an in-bounds and a one-past variant, and both builds must print and exit the same at -O2. A generated program must also exit cleanly or raise the bounds panic its variant predicts: a hang, a signal or any other panic fails the run. With --asan, the default build runs again under AddressSanitizer and UBSan and must end the same way. A failure prints its reproducer, the command that reruns it, and a minimised min.ts.

A weekly workflow, soundness-fuzz.yml, runs a longer seeded pass and uploads failing programs as a bounded artifact.

docs/security/codegen.md records the result: no unsound elision found, with the program count and the shapes covered.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: close the --emit-ts oracle: tsc --strict, the known-list pin, fuzz, and the docs
entries.body:
This is the last stage of the WP33 R3/R4 round trip. The TypeScript that --emit-ts writes now type-checks under `tsc --strict`, and the differential fuzzer runs the native build and the --emit-ts output and requires them to print and exit alike. The known list may hold only rows that are libm, ffi or refused, or that are host or range rows backed by evidence. CI's Node is pinned to 22.23.4, the version the list is regenerated under.

Generic code that nothing calls is translated without types:
- A body that needs no type is written as is.
- A body that does need a type becomes a stub that throws. In the program's own modules each stub comes with an NL8012 portability warning; std stubs are silent.
- A body that would make a choice depending on its type arguments (zero-filling `new Array<T>(n)`, or copying a record held inline) is refused with the new NL4014.

Also in this change:
- NL4013 now points at the node where two generic instances disagree.
- A runtime helper whose name the program uses itself is imported under an alias.
- The lazy argument of `expect` and `unwrapOr` stays lazy.
- `nish/runtime/node` no longer mutates global state: `process.argv` and `nish:process` imports go through `argv()`.
- Docs: SECRET-6 records what `wipe` cannot reach under Node. The CLI and to-TypeScript guide pages, LANGUAGE.md and the status lines say R3 and R4 are built.

entries.title: S6c's callgrind gate, and the owner's Q5 decision
entries.body:
The owner accepted S6c's structural-index design on 2026-10-24 (§8, Q5): one bitmap per 64-byte block, built in 4 KiB chunks into a fixed buffer kept across documents, with the kernel giving hints only and every error staying the scalar code's. It was to be built only if callgrind showed the 1.5x tokenize bar reachable on twitter.json and citm_catalog.json.

It does not. On main's tokenize loop, with the index priced by a throwaway AVX2/PCLMUL prototype of the kernel (2.06 instructions a byte on twitter, 1.90 on citm) and the walker at 8 instructions a mark, the instruction-count ceilings are 1.37x on twitter and 1.22x on citm. citm stays under the bar even with the kernel free (1.45x); twitter would need the kernel at or under 541,633 instructions a pass against 1,299,916 measured. So S6c is not built. docs/wp38-simd.md records the split, the sensitivities, and the kept work (stringInto, the grammar switch, numberF64) that would have to move first.

entries.title: attest build provenance, attach an SBOM, and rebuild releases from their tags
entries.body:
Every release now carries a build provenance attestation from actions/attest-build-provenance over each file in SHA256SUMS, with id-token and attestations write scoped to the release job. install.sh and scripts/fetch-seed.sh run `gh attestation verify` when gh is installed and signed in, refuse a release whose attestation gh rejects, and skip with a note when gh is missing, signed out or too old.

Each release also attaches an SPDX 2.3 SBOM written by scripts/sbom.mjs: every attached file with its SHA-256, the vendored code in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md, and the LLVM, Node and seed each tarball was built with.

A Rebuild workflow rebuilds the latest release weekly from its tag, seeded by the previous release, and compares through scripts/rebuild-compare.sh: the tarball's tree must match the tag's sources, and bin/nish must match once both copies lose .comment, whose toolchain version strings move with the runner. Linux rows gate; macOS rows report only.

Monthly, scripts/ddc-chain.sh builds every release tag from the ddc-0.6.0 root that TypeScript builds, each step seeded by the one before, and compares the end with the published x86_64-linux compiler (diverse double-compiling).

Fixes #389
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: hash and verify up to four bcrypt passwords at once, interleaved
entries.body:
`bcryptHash4` and `bcryptVerify4` compute up to four independent bcrypt
hashes in one call with their Blowfish encryptions interleaved, so the four
dependent S-box load chains overlap. Each lane's answer is byte for byte the
single path's.

A `Secret` cannot sit in an array or a field, so the batch takes fixed-arity
parameters: lane 0 is required, and lanes 1–3 are `Secret<u8[]> | null`.

All lanes' Blowfish state is one `Secret<u32[]>` that the call makes and wipes.
Each password reaches its lane through `exposeWith`. Verify groups lanes by
cost, and a malformed lane is an `Err` that names it.

The single path now builds its state in an array the hashing function
allocates itself, so a `std/threads` task can call `bcryptHash` and
`bcryptVerify`; the guide shows a server handing hashing to a worker thread.

The batch cannot yet run on a task, because a task's wipe of a `secret(...)`
value is a shared write (NL2471). That is recorded as BCRYPT-9, and a
follow-up checker change lifts it.
metrics: 4-lane 16.0 ms (15.8–16.4) CPU per cost-10 hash against tigokraft's 4-lane bcrypt.c clang -O2 -march=native 16.4 ms (16.2–16.9) and gcc 23.1 ms; single path 52.9 ms (52.3–53.1) against OpenBSD bcrypt.c clang -O2 54.1 ms (53.5–54.3); median of 5 rounds, min–max band

entries.title: harden every native binary the toolchain links
entries.body: Every native profile of scripts/build.sh, and so nish --link, nish run and the released nish, now links with full RELRO, a non-executable stack, PIE and stack-clash protection; IBT and the shadow stack on x86-64 (-fcf-protection=full), BTI and PAC on arm64 (-mbranch-protection=standard). The C runtime alone adds -fstack-protector-strong and, outside debug, -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3. Because clang reads no code-generation flags for a .ll input, the emitted IR carries the same protection as module flags and a "probe-stack" attribute, so every object agrees and the linker marks the binary. scripts/check-hardening.mjs reads the result back from ELF and Mach-O headers, in tests/run.js and in CI's bootstrap job. Recorded as RT-HARDEN in docs/security/runtime.md.
metrics: +328 to +1,136 B per speed binary; 12 of 14 benchmarks inside the ±1.5% band, cursor +6.1% and aes-gcm +3.6% from CET; strbuild +0.99% instructions, map-wordcount +0.11%, map-presize +0.24% from the stack protector

entries.title: Rng.nextInt answers an unbiased integer in a range
entries.body:
`Rng.nextInt(lo, hi)` in `nish/random` answers an `i32` in [lo, hi], both
ends included, each with equal chance, so a die is `r.nextInt(1, 6)` rather
than `(r.nextI32() >>> 1) % 6`, which leans toward the low faces. A draw
below 2^32 mod the span is refused and drawn again, so fewer than half are
ever refused; the whole `i32` range answers one `nextI32()`, and `lo > hi`
panics with `Rng.nextInt: lo is greater than hi`. The unsigned arithmetic is
spelled with `i32` operations that answer the same bits under Node, so a seed
answers the same integers natively and under the prelude. `nextI32` and
`nextF64` are unchanged, and every doc that rolls a die now uses `nextInt`.

entries.title: leave a wall of bricks in the help, and a door behind it
entries.body:
`nish --help` now shows a faint row of bricks under its title, with one brick knocked out. It is painted with the menu's own dim style, and is plain under NO_COLOR, in a pipe, or for an agent. Behind it, the undocumented `nish break` answers with a placeholder until the game ships. A few near-miss words get a riddle. A real file of either name still compiles as usual.

`nish/cli`'s `HelpMenu` gains the general-purpose `title(version, summary)` and `line(text)`. `header` now delegates to `title`.

entries.title: a std/threads task may wipe a Secret it made from a fresh value
entries.body:
A task's wipe of an array it allocated has been a local write since #894,
but a `Secret` made with `secret(...)` and wiped stayed a shared write
(NL2471). The bcrypt batch keeps its one state as a `Secret` of a fresh
array, so no task could call it.

`secret(v)` now counts as the function's own storage when `v` is
syntactically fresh (`new`, an array literal or an object literal holding
no shared value), the `Secret` is held by a `const`, and the same body
passes it straight to `wipe`. Every other `Secret` keeps today's facts:
- one made from a parameter, a field, a capture, a call's answer or a moved
  local;
- one bound by `let`;
- a borrowed parameter;
- a holder's field.

The wipe is still one volatile `llvm.memset`. The shared-write facts feed no
LLVM attribute, so the emitted IR does not change.

A string element handed to a call is now a read of its array, and a helper
writes below an argument only through a parameter it writes. Without those two
changes, a task calling `bcryptVerify4` read as writing the caller's
`hashes`.

`bcryptHash4` and `bcryptVerify4` now run on `std/threads` tasks, which
closes BCRYPT-9.

entries.title: S6d, the per-value cuts that would let S6c reach its bar
entries.body:
S6c's callgrind gate left the structural index at 1.37x on twitter and
1.22x on citm. S6d measured whether cutting the per-value work the index
keeps could lift that ceiling to 1.5x on both files, with the gate's Total
pinned to the record S6b left. It prices each candidate cut with a
throwaway prototype under callgrind and builds nothing.

A finer split of the kept work covers numberF64, stringInto and its memcpy
by length band, and next/value/key by part. On top of it come the cuts:
an integer path in numberF64, the innermost container's kind in a field,
whole-run copies in stringInto, a failed state in next's switch, the
grammar dispatch fused on the byte, and numberF64's sign read directly.
A saving that falls on work the gate already credits to the index is not
counted, so E2, K and M are left out.

Not reachable: twitter's best set reaches 1.533x and citm's best stops at
1.490x, 109,087 instructions short. The largest pool left open is citm's
second walk over a number's digits. The build and re-gate stages are not
started.

Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md (S6d row in §7; *S6d, the per-value cuts*)
Part of #952

entries.title: name the bcrypt single-path gap as LLVM's xor order
entries.body:
The single bcrypt hash trails gcc's build of OpenBSD's bcrypt.c by about
7%. The security record now shows why, with the instructions counted. Each
half-round computes x ^= P[n] ^ F(y). gcc keeps P[n] off the critical path,
(x ^ P[n]) ^ F(y), in all 16 half-rounds. LLVM does so only in the first:
Reassociate and a later InstCombine leave the other 15 as (P[n] ^ F(y)) ^ x,
one more dependent XOR after the last S-box add. clang's build of the same C
makes the same 15 of 16 choice, so the gap is LLVM 18 against gcc 13 (verdict
(a)), not Nish's codegen (b) or the std source shape (c). A straight-line
copy of the round and three other source orders give the same IR, so nothing
in std/ changes; no code changes.

Per half-round, Nish, gcc and clang each do 5 loads, 0 stores, 0 spills and
no checks, calls or jumps. The chain from y is 8 instructions and 12 cycles
for Nish and clang against 6 and 11 for gcc. That is 11.7, 10.9 and 11.9
measured cycles per half-round at 17,083,536 half-rounds per cost-10 hash.
The record carries one marked half-round from each listing, the objdump
recipe that prints the counts, the sha256 of each listing, and the wrapper
that reproduces the -print-changed trace.

Measured: Nish 71.5 (70.9-73.3) ms, gcc 66.8 (65.4-68.3) ms, clang 72.4 (72.3-73.8) ms per cost-10 hash, 5 interleaved rounds; no code change
Refs: docs/security/crypto-bcrypt.md#why-the-single-path-trails-gcc
Part of #953

entries.title: a Conduit server for the multicore server challenge
entries.body:
* fix(runtime): set TCP_NODELAY on every tcpConnect socket

tcpConnect left Nagle's algorithm on, so a client writing a small request
behind another waited on a delayed ACK. libpq and Go's net package turn it
off on every client socket; the runtime now does too, before connect, and a
refused option closes the socket and answers the error. bench/postgres drops
its hand-declared setsockopt workaround.

Fixes #942
Refs: docs/security/runtime.md (RT-22)
Tests: tests/cases/net_tcp_nodelay

* feat(net): a prefork supervisor that does not restart its workers

`PreforkConfig.restart`, on by default, can now be turned off. A worker
that exits then stays gone, and once none is left `preforkWith` answers
`PREFORK_WORKERS_EXITED` (-3), so a service under systemd or a
container runtime lets that restart policy decide instead of hiding a
crash loop behind its own. SIGTERM and SIGINT still stop the rest and
answer `PREFORK_STOPPED`.

Tests: tests/link/net_prefork_no_restart

* perf(net): walk the slots in Http1Server.expire only when one can be due

`expire` walked every slot up to the high-water mark on each call, so a
loop calling it every turn paid for every connection, idle or not, at
100,000 connections. A walk now records the soonest any slot can expire
(a slot's `lastActive` only grows, and a slot accepted later is due no
sooner than the shorter timeout from now), and a call before then
returns at once. `Http1TlsServer.expire` does the same. `expireScans`
counts the walks.

Tests: tests/link/net_http1_server

* perf(net): make an HTTP/1.1 slot's WebSocket decoder on its first upgrade

An Http1Connection used to allocate its WebSocket frame decoder (about
1.4 KiB of buffers) and a 125-byte pong buffer when it was built, so every
slot of a server paid for them whether or not it ever switched protocols.
The decoder is now made on the slot's first upgrade and kept for its later
peers, and the pong buffer on its first ping. With arena allocation, memory
not allocated is the only memory saved.

Measured: 3.93 -> 2.23 KiB RSS per idle keep-alive connection (8000 connections, one worker)
Tests: tests/link/net_http1_server

* test(bench): a full-seed PostgreSQL setup for the multicore challenge

bench/postgres/setup.sh takes PG_BENCH_SEED=full to load the challenge's
full seed (conduit_seed) beside the dev one, and bench/multicore/setup.sh
wraps it with a free-space check for the load that bench/multicore/run.sh
drives.

* test(bench): a Conduit server for the multicore server challenge

bench/multicore/conduit is a RealWorld Conduit server on nish/net's
Http1Server, PgPool, JsonWriter, the HMAC and bcrypt modules and prefork
with restarts off. Each HTTP worker binds the port with SO_REUSEPORT and
runs its own read and write pools; one more worker is the bcrypt service,
which the others reach over loopback TCP and which batches up to four
hashes or checks into bcryptHash4 or bcryptVerify4. The SQL is the
challenge's reference SQL. It passes the challenge's 197 conformance
checks on the dev seed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AGckAZ9R7km3KiYtkRsHj

* test(bench): drive the multicore server with the challenge's own load generator

bench/multicore/run.sh builds the Conduit server, runs the challenge's
conformance suite against it on a fresh dev database, then runs the
challenge's loadgen at fixed user counts on a fresh full-seed database
and reads /proc for the CPU every postgres process and every server
process used over the measured window, per completed request. It ends
with the server's RSS per idle keep-alive connection.

The article a create reads back is found by a scalar subquery over
currval, which the planner runs once: compared with each row's id, the
volatile call scanned the whole primary key and held the write
connection for over a second under load.

bench/multicore/submission/nish-std-amritk is the folder the challenge
receives: install.sh (LLVM 18 from apt, a checked Node.js 22.18.0 tarball
and nish 0.22.0 from npm), build.sh, start.sh, the MIT licence and a

* feat(net): lend an idle HTTP/1.1 slot's input buffers back to the server

Http1Config.idleInput, off by default, makes a slot that has answered its
request and holds no byte of the next give its parser's input and head

next byte, so their memory follows the connections mid-request rather
than every keep-alive connection open. Http1Parser makes both buffers on
first use instead of in its constructor, so a slot that lends them never
allocates its own.

* perf(bench): commit the Conduit server's writes in groups

Writes wait in a ring until the write connection has no batch in flight,
then up to 128 go as one pipelined group: one implicit transaction, one
WAL flush, each answer written into the request's own buffer and sent
once the group's ReadyForQuery says it committed. A group that fails has
rolled back every write in it, so each is sent again alone; a group lost
with its connection may have committed, so its writes answer 500 and are
not sent again. No timer: an idle server sends a write at once.

* perf(bench): batch the Conduit server's reads into shared groups

The group-commit ring now serves both pools. Up to 32 reads waiting while
a read connection is busy go out as one pipelined group, one implicit
transaction, so Postgres starts and ends one transaction for all of them
rather than one each; a read is answered as soon as its last statement
completes. A failed group sends each read it skipped again alone; a read
lost with its connection is sent again once, alone.

* fix(bench): recover the Conduit write pool from a half-built group

A bind refused part way leaves the pool's group open with a bind in it,
which no Sync can end, so the pool waited on it for good. The batch
budget keeps that from happening inside one batch, but resends of a
failed batch's writes queue beside it unbudgeted. When the binds wrote
and the send then fails, the worker now drops that connection and makes
it again, as on a socket error. A refusal that wrote nothing (the pool
has already discarded the group) keeps the connection. With the budget
lifted, sixteen ~900 KB creates at once answer five 500s and the next
write 201, where the pool had stopped.

Tests: conformance 197/197; concurrency and large-write checks on a live server

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AGckAZ9R7km3KiYtkRsHj

* fix(bench): end a half-built Conduit bind instead of dropping its connection

The last commit dropped the write connection when a group was left open
with a bind in it, but it detected that from the connection's queued
bytes, which an open bind hides, so a single request refused part way
through its parameters still stalled the pool. Now the worker ends any
bind left open with the parameters it has (`bindEnd` is never refused
for room). Postgres refuses the short bind ("bind message supplies 3
parameters, but prepared statement "article_create" requires 4"), the
group fails and rolls back, and the Sync ends it, so the connection and
its other groups are kept. With the batch budget lifted, sixteen ~900 KB
creates at once answer their 500s and the next write 201.

Tests: conformance 197/197; concurrency and large-write checks on a live server

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012AGckAZ9R7km3KiYtkRsHj

* fix(bench): hold back a Conduit write that would not fit rather than fail it

A write's bind refused for room failed the group, or, when it was refused
at its start, sent the writes bound before it while every request in the
batch answered 500, so writes that committed were reported as failed.
bindAll now checks each write's upper-bound bind size (twice its text and
512 bytes) against what already waits on the connection before binding
it. The group ends before a write that might not fit, and that write and
the ones after it go again at the end of the pump, once the output has
been sent. A bind is never refused for room, and no write answers 500
for want of it. With the batch budget lifted, forty ~900 KB creates at
once and a write after them all answer 201, with 41 rows stored.

The bindEnd recovery stays for a bind refused for any other reason.

Tests: conformance 197/197; concurrency and large-write checks on a live server
